title: Index Funds vs Active Funds in India: Which Should You Pick?

content:
For most Indian investors, index funds are the better bet for large-cap exposure. SPIVA India data spanning a decade shows that a clear majority of active large-cap mutual funds underperform their benchmarks once you account for fees. The expense ratio gap, running about 1.3 to 1.8 percentage points a year, is the main culprit. In mid-cap and small-cap segments, active funds have a meaningfully better track record.

Key Takeaways

  • A majority of active large-cap mutual funds underperformed the Nifty 50 benchmark over 10 years, per SPIVA India data.
  • Index funds charge 0.1 to 0.2% annually; active large-cap funds typically charge 1.5 to 2%, a gap that compounds sharply over time.
  • Active mid-cap and small-cap funds beat their benchmarks more often, especially in 2025, per SPIVA year-end data.
  • Passive fund AUM in India crossed roughly ₹11 lakh crore in 2026, up from ₹2.8 lakh crore in 2020.
  • Practical starting point: a Nifty 50 index fund as your core, with active funds only in mid or small-cap if you want that exposure.

Should you choose an index fund or an active fund?

For large-cap in India, index funds win most of the time. The expense ratio gap, typically 1.3 to 1.8 percentage points per year, is a consistent headwind that most active managers can't earn back. In mid-cap and small-cap, analyst coverage is thinner, markets are less efficient, and active managers have shown a better shot at outperforming.

The pitch for active funds is that a skilled manager, doing deep research, can beat the market. It's a fair argument. But in the large-cap space, every major Nifty 50 stock is followed by dozens of analysts at every large brokerage. New information gets priced in fast. Outperforming consistently is genuinely difficult. And you're paying 1.5 to 2% a year for the attempt, every year, regardless of outcome.

This shift has occured gradually in the industry, as more long-term performance data became available. Retail investors started comparing their active fund returns against what a plain index fund would have delivered, and the numbers weren't flattering.

Why do most active large-cap funds fail to beat the market?

Fees are the main reason. Active large-cap funds charge 1.5 to 2% annually, while a Nifty 50 index fund charges 0.1 to 0.2%. That gap must be recovered through outperformance before you see any advantage. SPIVA data shows most active large-cap funds don't manage it over a decade.

There's also a structural problem. As a fund grows in assets, it becomes harder to make high-conviction bets. A very large fund buying into a mid-size company moves the price against itself before it finishes the trade. Some of the top-performing funds from a decade ago are now so large that the strategy behind their old track record isn't really available to them anymore.

A fund with a high expense ratio isn't definately going to underperform, but the math stacks against it over the long run. A manager who beats the market by 1% a year before fees ends up delivering nothing extra in a fund charging 1.5%. Beating by 1% consistently for a decade is rare.

Index Funds vs Active Funds: A Quick Comparison

This covers large-cap funds, where the difference is sharpest.

10-year benchmark beat rateTracks benchmark (by design)Majority underperform (SPIVA)
Manager riskNone (rules-based)Affected by manager changes
Holdings transparencyAlways known (Nifty 50 stocks)Disclosed monthly
Best suited forLong-term core holdingNiche or satellite exposure

Where do active funds still have an edge?

In mid-cap and small-cap segments. SPIVA India's year-end 2025 data shows active mid-cap and small-cap funds delivered majority outperformance in 2025, their best relative showing since 2014. In these segments, companies are less covered by analysts, pricing is less efficient, and a manager who does thorough research can sometimes find value the market hasn't priced in yet.

The same fee math still applies. You need the manager to beat by enough to cover the extra 1 to 1.5% in annual fees, and then some. So even in mid and small-cap, the right question is: has this specific fund actually beaten its benchmark by more than its expense ratio, over a period long enough to matter?

ELSS funds (the Section 80C tax-saving options) often come up here. Many are actively managed. But index-linked ELSS funds exist now, so it's worth comparing before defaulting to an active one.

How should you actually decide?

If you're starting out with equity mutual funds, begin with a Nifty 50 index fund. Low fee, no manager risk. For mid-cap or small-cap exposure, active funds with a 5-year track record and expense ratio under 1.5% are worth a look. Compare your active fund's actual returns against its benchmark before assuming it's earning its cost.

Say you've been putting ₹5,000 a month into an active large-cap fund for a few years and notice the expense ratio is 1.8%. Compare its 5-year returns to the Nifty 50. If it hasn't beaten the index by at least 1.8% a year on average, you've been paying for underperformance. Switching doesn't mean exiting the market, just redirecting future SIP installments.

The one group that can skip this debate: anyone whose equity exposure is only through EPF and NPS. Those are managed separately with their own return structure. The index-vs-active question becomes relevant when you're adding equity mutual funds on top of those.

This is general information, not personalized financial advice. Your tax situation, investment horizon, and risk tolerance should guide specific decisions.

Frequently asked questions

Are index funds safe in India?

Index funds carry the same market risk as the stocks they track. A Nifty 50 index fund falls when markets fall. What they remove is manager risk and unnecessary fee drag. Over long horizons, that combination has outperformed most active large-cap alternatives in India.

Can an active fund beat an index fund over 10 years?

Some do. The problem is picking the right one in advance. SPIVA data shows that over 10 years, a majority of active large-cap funds in India underperformed their benchmark. A few outperform significantly, but identifying them beforehand, rather than just following past returns, is harder than most fund brochures suggest.

Is a 2% expense ratio too high for a mutual fund?

For a large-cap fund, almost certainly yes. A 2% annual charge requires the manager to beat the market by 2% every year just to match a zero-cost index fund. For a mid-cap or small-cap fund with a strong 5-year track record, 1 to 1.5% is more defensible, but still worth scrutinizing.

Should I switch from my active fund to an index fund?

Compare your fund's 5-year returns against its benchmark first. If it has consistently underperformed by less than its expense ratio, switching to an index fund makes financial sense. Also check whether the switch triggers short-term capital gains tax, which might affect timing but not the underlying logic.

Which Nifty 50 index fund should I look at first?

UTI Nifty 50 Index Fund and HDFC Index Fund Nifty 50 Plan are among the established options, both with expense ratios around 0.1 to 0.2% and long track records. Compare tracking error before picking: lower tracking error means the fund closely follows the actual Nifty 50 index.

The short version

For large-cap investing in India, index funds beat most active alternatives, primarily because of fees. For mid-cap and small-cap, active funds have a better record, but check whether your specific fund has actually earned its higher cost. Start with a Nifty 50 index fund as the core of your equity portfolio. Add active funds only in segments where the data gives them a real edge.
